body:
Displaying bundle size accurately is a difficult problem. If you only use one single component from the library, then it’s fully accurate. However once you start using multiple components, the numbers become inaccurate as the sizes don’t add up simply/cumulatively as displayed due to shared dependencies/logic/compression, etc.

I propose we take a non-naive approach to this. https://bundlejs.com allows you to export the specific components you're actually using, treeshaking enabled, to see a true picture. We could have a UI for this on the website where they select all the components they're using/will decide to use to get a true picture of the bundle size.
Oh, I forgot I had opened https://github.com/mui/material-ui/issues/40591. The best I could figure out in the past was https://github.com/pastelsky/bundlephobia/issues/389.

Something Radix did well was allowing you to install just the parts you needed, if you want the select component you run `npm install @radix-ui/react-select` and that's all you get (with it's dependencies of course). This also means I can look at the [npm page](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@radix-ui/react-select) and see that the component is going to cost 328 kB. I will say they could do some work to make each npm page feel like it's real when it's too bare it feels like somewhere you've ended up by mistake.

By comparison if I want to use the base-ui select (`@base-ui-components/react/select`) I have to get the whole of `@base-ui-components/react` which I know rationally will treeshake on build but at a glance looking at the [npm page](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@base-ui-components/react) I see 3.48 MB which feels like a 10× increase.

By splitting up each component you get people to see they can cherry pick the bits they want and you get the added bonus of seeing the sizes on npm for "free".

> By splitting up each component you get people to see they can cherry pick the bits they want and you get the added bonus of seeing the sizes on npm for "free".

In practice, cherry-picking the components you need works much better with monopackage tree-shaking: splitting up components into separate packages causes difficult bugs with version mismatches (dot point 3): https://github.com/mui/base-ui/issues/1700#issuecomment-2795706339

Radix's docs have the issue outlined in https://github.com/mui/base-ui/issues/602#issuecomment-2345217478. Each component page having a size cost is misleading if you were to add them together cumulatively, as in real apps you're likely using multiple ones that are highly interdependent.

For instance Menu and Select share many dependencies that individually have a large upfront cost but when you actually use them together, the cumulative cost is much less than adding their individual costs. 

This is why exporting what you need and seeing the resulting production bundle is best. Here's an example of Base UI latest canary with a Vite project:
```
# Baseline: 
dist/assets/index-55j1Zgeo.js   143.62 kB │ gzip: 46.09 kB

# All Menu features:
dist/assets/index-BbpivL1E.js   256.11 kB │ gzip: 84.61 kB

# All Select features:
dist/assets/index-JemfAkez.js   255.15 kB │ gzip: 84.40 kB

# All Select and Menu combined:
dist/assets/index-D6lmjh9y.js   282.85 kB │ gzip: 92.58 kB
```

I wouldn't consider the npm package install size a relevant metric though unless it's so huge that it affects install times - it only represents the cost to your disk space, which is a lot less important than the cost of end users downloading your JS bundle

I do agree, my only thought here was this issue seemed to be more about optics and getting rid of the "bloated" reputation. People like to see small numbers even if those numbers don't mean much in practice 🤷.
